claim: Craniosynostosis affects 1 in 2000 newborns.
source: Premature fusion of the cranial sutures (craniosynostosis), affecting 1 in 2000 newborns, is treated surgically in infancy to prevent adverse neurologic outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement of disease prevalence presented in the abstract without supporting data in the manuscript itself.

claim: Craniosynostosis is treated surgically in infancy to prevent adverse neurologic outcomes.
source: Premature fusion of the cranial sutures (craniosynostosis), affecting 1 in 2000 newborns, is treated surgically in infancy to prevent adverse neurologic outcomes.
evidence: This is a statement about clinical practice presented without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Exome sequencing was performed on 132 parent-offspring trios and 59 additional probands with non-syndromic midline craniosynostosis.
source: To identify mutations contributing to common non-syndromic midline (sagittal and metopic) craniosynostosis, we performed exome sequencing of 132 parent-offspring trios and 59 additional probands.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and sample size of the study.

claim: Thirteen probands (7%) had damaging de novo or rare transmitted mutations in SMAD6.
source: Thirteen probands (7%) had damaging de novo or rare transmitted mutations in SMAD6, an inhibitor of BMP – induced osteoblast differentiation (p<10−20).
evidence: This is a direct result from the exome sequencing analysis with statistical support.

claim: SMAD6 is an inhibitor of BMP-induced osteoblast differentiation.
source: Thirteen probands (7%) had damaging de novo or rare transmitted mutations in SMAD6, an inhibitor of BMP – induced osteoblast differentiation (p<10−20).
evidence: This is a statement about the biological function of SMAD6 based on established knowledge.

claim: The association between SMAD6 mutations and craniosynostosis is statistically significant with p<10^-20.
source: Thirteen probands (7%) had damaging de novo or rare transmitted mutations in SMAD6, an inhibitor of BMP – induced osteoblast differentiation (p<10−20).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis of mutations in the cohort.

claim: SMAD6 mutations showed incomplete penetrance of less than 60%.
source: SMAD6 mutations nonetheless showed striking incomplete penetrance (<60%).
evidence: This is an observation from the pedigree analysis of families with SMAD6 mutations.

claim: A common variant near BMP2 is strongly associated with midline craniosynostosis.
source: Genotypes of a common variant near BMP2 that is strongly associated with midline craniosynostosis explained nearly all the phenotypic variation in these kindreds, with highly significant evidence of genetic interaction between these loci via both association and analysis of linkage.
evidence: This refers to prior GWAS findings and the current study's analysis of this variant in SMAD6 mutation carriers.

claim: Genotypes of a common variant near BMP2 explained nearly all the phenotypic variation in kindreds with SMAD6 mutations.
source: Genotypes of a common variant near BMP2 that is strongly associated with midline craniosynostosis explained nearly all the phenotypic variation in these kindreds, with highly significant evidence of genetic interaction between these loci via both association and analysis of linkage.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of BMP2 genotypes in families with SMAD6 mutations.

claim: There is highly significant evidence of genetic interaction between SMAD6 and BMP2 loci via both association and linkage analysis.
source: Genotypes of a common variant near BMP2 that is strongly associated with midline craniosynostosis explained nearly all the phenotypic variation in these kindreds, with highly significant evidence of genetic interaction between these loci via both association and analysis of linkage.
evidence: This is a conclusion from statistical analyses of genetic data.

claim: The epistatic interaction of rare SMAD6 variants and common BMP2 variants defines the most frequent cause of midline craniosynostosis.
source: This epistatic interaction of rare and common variants defines the most frequent cause of midline craniosynostosis and has implications for the genetic basis of other diseases.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the frequency of these genotypes in the cohort.

claim: Brain volume doubles in the first year of life.
source: The cranial sutures are not fused at birth, allowing for doubling of brain volume in the first year of life and continued growth through adolescence (Persing et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a statement about normal development supported by a citation.

claim: The metopic suture normally closes between 6 and 12 months.
source: The metopic suture normally closes between 6 and 12 months, while the sagittal, coronal, and lambdoid sutures typically fuse in adulthood (Persing et al., 1989; Weinzweig et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about normal cranial development supported by citations.

claim: The sagittal, coronal, and lambdoid sutures typically fuse in adulthood.
source: The metopic suture normally closes between 6 and 12 months, while the sagittal, coronal, and lambdoid sutures typically fuse in adulthood (Persing et al., 1989; Weinzweig et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a statement about normal cranial development supported by citations.

claim: Premature fusion of cranial sutures can result in brain compression and suture-specific craniofacial dysmorphism.
source: Premature fusion of any of these sutures can result in brain compression and suture-specific craniofacial dysmorphism (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the consequences of craniosynostosis, with reference to Figure 1 showing examples.

claim: Syndromic forms of craniosynostosis have prevalence of approximately 1/60,000 to 1/1,000,000 live births.
source: Studies of syndromic forms of craniosynostosis, each with prevalence of ~1/60,000 to 1/1,000,000 live births and collectively accounting for 15–20% of all cases, have implicated mutations in more than 50 genes (Twigg and Wilkie, 2015; Flaherty et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about disease prevalence supported by citations.

claim: Syndromic craniosynostosis collectively accounts for 15-20% of all craniosynostosis cases.
source: Studies of syndromic forms of craniosynostosis, each with prevalence of ~1/60,000 to 1/1,000,000 live births and collectively accounting for 15–20% of all cases, have implicated mutations in more than 50 genes (Twigg and Wilkie, 2015; Flaherty et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about the proportion of syndromic cases supported by citations.

claim: More than 50 genes have been implicated in syndromic craniosynostosis.
source: Studies of syndromic forms of craniosynostosis, each with prevalence of ~1/60,000 to 1/1,000,000 live births and collectively accounting for 15–20% of all cases, have implicated mutations in more than 50 genes (Twigg and Wilkie, 2015; Flaherty et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a summary of prior research supported by citations.

claim: Mutations that increase MAPK/ERK signaling cause rare syndromic coronal or multisuture craniosynostosis.
source: For example, mutations that increase MAPK/ERK signaling (e.g. FGFR1-3 (Twigg and Wilkie, 2015; Flaherty et al., 2016), ERF [Twigg et al., 2013]) cause rare syndromic coronal or multisuture craniosynostosis, while mutations that perturb SMAD signaling (e.g. TGFBR1/2 [Loeys et al., 2005], SKI [Doyle et al., 2012], RUNX2 [Mefford et al., 2010; Javed et al., 2008]) cause rare syndromes involving the midline (sagittal and metopic) sutures.
evidence: This is a statement about genetic causes of syndromic craniosynostosis supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutations in FGFR1-3 and ERF increase MAPK/ERK signaling.
source: For example, mutations that increase MAPK/ERK signaling (e.g. FGFR1-3 (Twigg and Wilkie, 2015; Flaherty et al., 2016), ERF [Twigg et al., 2013]) cause rare syndromic coronal or multisuture craniosynostosis, while mutations that perturb SMAD signaling (e.g. TGFBR1/2 [Loeys et al., 2005], SKI [Doyle et al., 2012], RUNX2 [Mefford et al., 2010; Javed et al., 2008]) cause rare syndromes involving the midline (sagittal and metopic) sutures.
evidence: This is a statement about the molecular effects of specific mutations supported by citations.

claim: Mutations that perturb SMAD signaling cause rare syndromes involving the midline (sagittal and metopic) sutures.
source: For example, mutations that increase MAPK/ERK signaling (e.g. FGFR1-3 (Twigg and Wilkie, 2015; Flaherty et al., 2016), ERF [Twigg et al., 2013]) cause rare syndromic coronal or multisuture craniosynostosis, while mutations that perturb SMAD signaling (e.g. TGFBR1/2 [Loeys et al., 2005], SKI [Doyle et al., 2012], RUNX2 [Mefford et al., 2010; Javed et al., 2008]) cause rare syndromes involving the midline (sagittal and metopic) sutures.
evidence: This is a statement about genetic causes of midline craniosynostosis supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mutations in TGFBR1/2, SKI, and RUNX2 perturb SMAD signaling.
source: For example, mutations that increase MAPK/ERK signaling (e.g. FGFR1-3 (Twigg and Wilkie, 2015; Flaherty et al., 2016), ERF [Twigg et al., 2013]) cause rare syndromic coronal or multisuture craniosynostosis, while mutations that perturb SMAD signaling (e.g. TGFBR1/2 [Loeys et al., 2005], SKI [Doyle et al., 2012], RUNX2 [Mefford et al., 2010; Javed et al., 2008]) cause rare syndromes involving the midline (sagittal and metopic) sutures.
evidence: This is a statement about the molecular effects of specific mutations supported by citations.

claim: Aberrant signaling in cranial neural crest cells during craniofacial development has been suggested as a common mechanism for premature suture fusion.
source: While the detailed pathophysiology of premature suture fusion has not been elucidated, aberrant signaling in cranial neural crest cells during craniofacial development has been suggested as a common mechanism (Mishina and Snider, 2014; Komatsu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a statement about a proposed mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Mutations in genes causing syndromic craniosynostosis are very rarely found in non-syndromic craniosynostosis.
source: Despite success in identifying the genes underlying rare syndromic craniosynostosis, mutations in these genes are very rarely found in their non-syndromic counterparts (Boyadjiev and International Craniosynostosis Consortium, 2007).
evidence: This is a statement about the genetic differences between syndromic and non-syndromic forms supported by a citation.

claim: Non-syndromic craniosynostosis of the midline sutures accounts for 50% of all craniosynostosis.
source: Non-syndromic craniosynostosis of the midline sutures account for 50% of all craniosynostosis (Slater et al., 2008; Greenwood et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about disease prevalence supported by citations.

claim: A GWAS of non-syndromic sagittal craniosynostosis has implicated common variants in a segment of a gene desert approximately 345 kb downstream of BMP2.
source: A GWAS of non-syndromic sagittal craniosynostosis has implicated common variants in a segment of a gene desert ~345 kb downstream of BMP2, and within an intron of BBS9; these risk alleles have unusually large effect (odds ratios > 4 at each locus) (Justice et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about prior GWAS findings supported by a citation.

claim: A GWAS of non-syndromic sagittal craniosynostosis has implicated common variants within an intron of BBS9.
source: A GWAS of non-syndromic sagittal craniosynostosis has implicated common variants in a segment of a gene desert ~345 kb downstream of BMP2, and within an intron of BBS9; these risk alleles have unusually large effect (odds ratios > 4 at each locus) (Justice et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about prior GWAS findings supported by a citation.

claim: Risk alleles near BMP2 and in BBS9 have unusually large effect with odds ratios greater than 4 at each locus.
source: A GWAS of non-syndromic sagittal craniosynostosis has implicated common variants in a segment of a gene desert ~345 kb downstream of BMP2, and within an intron of BBS9; these risk alleles have unusually large effect (odds ratios > 4 at each locus) (Justice et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a statement about the effect size of genetic variants from prior GWAS supported by a citation.

claim: Rare alleles with large effect have not been identified to date in non-syndromic sagittal or metopic craniosynostosis prior to this study.
source: Nonetheless, rare alleles with large effect have not been identified to date in non-syndromic sagittal or metopic craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: The cohort included 191 probands with non-syndromic midline craniosynostosis.
source: We recruited a cohort of 191 probands with non-syndromic midline craniosynostosis, including 132 parent-offspring trios and 59 probands with one parent, along with selected extended family members (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the study cohort composition.

claim: The cohort included 113 probands with isolated sagittal craniosynostosis.
source: All probands had undergone reconstructive surgery for either isolated sagittal (n = 113), metopic (n = 70) or combined sagittal and metopic (n = 8) craniosynostosis.
evidence: This describes the phenotypic breakdown of the cohort.

claim: The cohort included 70 probands with metopic craniosynostosis.
source: All probands had undergone reconstructive surgery for either isolated sagittal (n = 113), metopic (n = 70) or combined sagittal and metopic (n = 8) craniosynostosis.
evidence: This describes the phenotypic breakdown of the cohort.

claim: The cohort included 8 probands with combined sagittal and metopic craniosynostosis.
source: All probands had undergone reconstructive surgery for either isolated sagittal (n = 113), metopic (n = 70) or combined sagittal and metopic (n = 8) craniosynostosis.
evidence: This describes the phenotypic breakdown of the cohort.

claim: Seventeen kindreds had 1 to 3 additional affected family members.
source: Seventeen kindreds had 1 to 3 additional affected family members, including 7 parents, 12 siblings, 3 aunts/uncles and 4 more distant relatives of probands.
evidence: This describes the familial nature of some cases in the cohort.

claim: A total of 144 de novo mutations were identified in 132 trios.
source: We identified a total of 144 de novo mutations, providing a de novo mutation rate of 1.64 × 10–8 per base pair, and 1.09 de novo mutations in the coding region per offspring, consistent with prior experimental results and expectation (Ware et al., 2015; Homsy et al., 2015) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a result from the exome sequencing analysis.

claim: The de novo mutation rate was 1.64 × 10^-8 per base pair.
source: We identified a total of 144 de novo mutations, providing a de novo mutation rate of 1.64 × 10–8 per base pair, and 1.09 de novo mutations in the coding region per offspring, consistent with prior experimental results and expectation (Ware et al., 2015; Homsy et al., 2015) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a calculated rate from the sequencing data.

claim: There were 1.09 de novo mutations in the coding region per offspring.
source: We identified a total of 144 de novo mutations, providing a de novo mutation rate of 1.64 × 10–8 per base pair, and 1.09 de novo mutations in the coding region per offspring, consistent with prior experimental results and expectation (Ware et al., 2015; Homsy et al., 2015) (Table 1).
evidence: This is a calculated rate from the sequencing data that matches prior expectations.

claim: There was significant enrichment of protein-altering mutations compared to expectation.
source: Comparison of the observed distribution of mutation types to the expected from the Poisson distribution demonstrated significant enrichment of protein-altering mutations, predominantly accounted for by an excess of damaging missense mutations (MetaSVM D-mis; 28 observed D-mis compared to 14.5 expected, p=1.0 × 10–3, 1.93-fold enrichment), with a corresponding paucity of silent mutations (21 compared to 40.4 expected, p=3.0 × 10–4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from comparing observed to expected mutation distributions.

claim: There were 28 observed damaging missense mutations compared to 14.5 expected (p=1.0 × 10^-3, 1.93-fold enrichment).
source: Comparison of the observed distribution of mutation types to the expected from the Poisson distribution demonstrated significant enrichment of protein-altering mutations, predominantly accounted for by an excess of damaging missense mutations (MetaSVM D-mis; 28 observed D-mis compared to 14.5 expected, p=1.0 × 10–3, 1.93-fold enrichment), with a corresponding paucity of silent mutations (21 compared to 40.4 expected, p=3.0 × 10–4).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result from the mutation analysis.

claim: There were 21 silent mutations compared to 40.4 expected (p=3.0 × 10^-4).
source: Comparison of the observed distribution of mutation types to the expected from the Poisson distribution demonstrated significant enrichment of protein-altering mutations, predominantly accounted for by an excess of damaging missense mutations (MetaSVM D-mis; 28 observed D-mis compared to 14.5 expected, p=1.0 × 10–3, 1.93-fold enrichment), with a corresponding paucity of silent mutations (21 compared to 40.4 expected, p=3.0 × 10–4).
evidence: This is a specific statistical result showing fewer silent mutations than expected.

claim: De novo mutations contribute to approximately 15% of non-syndromic midline craniosynostosis.
source: From the difference in the observed vs. expected number of de novo protein-altering mutations per subject, we infer that these de novo mutations contribute to ~15% of non-syndromic midline craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is an inference from the excess of protein-altering de novo mutations.

claim: SMAD6 harbored three de novo mutations including two inferred loss of function mutations and one damaging missense mutation.
source: Analysis of de novo mutation burden revealed that a single gene, SMAD6, harbored three de novo mutations, including two inferred loss of function (LOF) mutations (p.Q78fs*41 and p.E374*) and one D-mis mutation (p.G390C).
evidence: This is a direct result from the de novo mutation analysis.

claim: All three SMAD6 de novo mutations were heterozygous.
source: All three were heterozygous and occurred in families in which the proband was the sole affected member.
evidence: This describes the zygosity of the identified mutations.

claim: The three SMAD6 de novo mutations occurred in families in which the proband was the sole affected member.
source: All three were heterozygous and occurred in families in which the proband was the sole affected member.
evidence: This describes the family history of cases with de novo SMAD6 mutations.

claim: Two de novo SMAD6 mutations occurred in probands and one occurred in an unaffected mother of a proband.
source: Two de novo mutations occurred in probands and one occurred in an unaffected mother of a proband (Figure 2).
evidence: This describes where the de novo mutations arose, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: TTN was the only other gene with more than one protein altering de novo mutation.
source: TTN, which encodes the largest human protein, was the only other gene with more than one protein altering de novo mutation, and both of these were predicted by MetaSVM to encode tolerated variants (p.I3580M, p.T19373S).
evidence: This is a result from the de novo mutation analysis.

claim: Both TTN de novo mutations were predicted by MetaSVM to encode tolerated variants.
source: TTN, which encodes the largest human protein, was the only other gene with more than one protein altering de novo mutation, and both of these were predicted by MetaSVM to encode tolerated variants (p.I3580M, p.T19373S).
evidence: This is a result from computational prediction of variant effects.

claim: The probability of seeing at least two de novo LOFs and one missense mutation in SMAD6 by chance was 3.6 × 10^-9.
source: From the prior probability of de novo mutation of each base in SMAD6 and the impact on the encoded protein (Samocha et al., 2014), the probability of seeing at least two de novo LOFs and one missense mutation by chance in a cohort of this size was 3.6 × 10–9 (Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical calculation based on mutation probabilities.

claim: Observing two or more de novo LOF mutations in any gene in this cohort was not expected by chance (p=8.4 × 10^-3).
source: Similarly, observing two or more de novo LOF mutations in any gene in this cohort was not expected by chance (p=8.4 × 10–3, see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statistical result from permutation analysis.

claim: SMAD6 is not unusually mutable.
source: Lastly, SMAD6 is not unusually mutable, as we found no de novo SMAD6 mutations in 900 control trios comprising healthy siblings of individuals with autism (Iossifov et al., 2014; O'Roak et al., 2011; Sanders et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a result from comparison to control cohorts.

claim: No de novo SMAD6 mutations were found in 900 control trios comprising healthy siblings of individuals with autism.
source: Lastly, SMAD6 is not unusually mutable, as we found no de novo SMAD6 mutations in 900 control trios comprising healthy siblings of individuals with autism (Iossifov et al., 2014; O'Roak et al., 2011; Sanders et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a result from analysis of control data.

claim: Among 191 probands, there were 1135 rare LOF and 3156 rare damaging alleles.
source: Among 191 probands, we found 1135 rare LOF and 3156 rare damaging (LOF + D-mis) alleles.
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of rare variants in probands.

claim: The expected number of rare LOF alleles in SMAD6 in probands was 0.05, and the observed number was 8 (p=1.1 × 10^-15, 156-fold enrichment).
source: The expected number of rare LOF alleles in SMAD6 in probands was 0.05, and the observed number was 8 (p=1.1 × 10–15, 156-fold enrichment).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the rare variant burden analysis.

claim: There were 13 rare damaging variants in SMAD6 compared to 0.14 expected (p=1.3 × 10^-21, 91.4-fold enrichment).
source: Similarly, there were 13 rare damaging variants in SMAD6 compared to 0.14 expected (p=1.3 × 10–21, 91.4-fold enrichment).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the rare variant burden analysis.

claim: All SMAD6 variants were heterozygous and different from one another.
source: All of these SMAD6 variants were confirmed by direct Sanger sequencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). All were heterozygous and different from one another (Figure 2—source data 1); 11 were absent among >105 alleles in the ExAC database, while two were previously seen, each once in ExAC (p.E407* and p.R465C, ExAC allele frequencies 9.0 × 10–6 and 9.4 × 10–6 respectively).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the identified SMAD6 variants.

claim: Eleven SMAD6 variants were absent among >10^5 alleles in the ExAC database.
source: All of these SMAD6 variants were confirmed by direct Sanger sequencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). All were heterozygous and different from one another (Figure 2—source data 1); 11 were absent among >105 alleles in the ExAC database, while two were previously seen, each once in ExAC (p.E407* and p.R465C, ExAC allele frequencies 9.0 × 10–6 and 9.4 × 10–6 respectively).
evidence: This describes the rarity of the identified variants based on population databases.

claim: Two SMAD6 variants were previously seen once each in ExAC (p.E407* and p.R465C, with allele frequencies 9.0 × 10^-6 and 9.4 × 10^-6 respectively).
source: All of these SMAD6 variants were confirmed by direct Sanger sequencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 2). All were heterozygous and different from one another (Figure 2—source data 1); 11 were absent among >105 alleles in the ExAC database, while two were previously seen, each once in ExAC (p.E407* and p.R465C, ExAC allele frequencies 9.0 × 10–6 and 9.4 × 10–6 respectively).
evidence: This describes the frequency of two variants in population databases.

claim: Eight of the 13 rare heterozygous damaging variants in SMAD6 are frameshift or premature termination mutations.
source: The fact that eight of the 13 rare heterozygous damaging variants in SMAD6 seen in our cohort are frameshift (n = 5) or premature termination (n = 3) mutations, which are distributed throughout the encoded protein (Figure 2a), strongly supports haploinsufficiency as the mechanism of the genetic contribution of SMAD6 to craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is a result from characterizing the types of mutations identified.

claim: The distribution of LOF mutations throughout SMAD6 strongly supports haploinsufficiency as the mechanism of genetic contribution to craniosynostosis.
source: The fact that eight of the 13 rare heterozygous damaging variants in SMAD6 seen in our cohort are frameshift (n = 5) or premature termination (n = 3) mutations, which are distributed throughout the encoded protein (Figure 2a), strongly supports haploinsufficiency as the mechanism of the genetic contribution of SMAD6 to craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is an inference from the types and distribution of mutations observed.

claim: All 17 affected subjects in kindreds with SMAD6 mutations had the SMAD6 mutation found in the proband.
source: Within the 13 kindreds harboring rare damaging SMAD6 variants, all 17 affected subjects had the SMAD6 mutation found in the proband (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a result from segregation analysis in families.

claim: Zero of 10 parental SMAD6 mutation carriers had a diagnosis of or showed evidence of craniosynostosis.
source: In particular, zero of 10 parental SMAD6 mutation carriers had a diagnosis of, or showed evidence of craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is an observation demonstrating incomplete penetrance.

claim: The penetrance of SMAD6 mutations is estimated at 24% following exclusion of probands.
source: From the data in these kindreds, the penetrance of SMAD6 mutations is estimated at 24% following exclusion of probands, who were ascertained for the presence of disease (57% if probands are included).
evidence: This is a calculated estimate from the family data.

claim: The penetrance of SMAD6 mutations is 57% if probands are included.
source: From the data in these kindreds, the penetrance of SMAD6 mutations is estimated at 24% following exclusion of probands, who were ascertained for the presence of disease (57% if probands are included).
evidence: This is a calculated estimate from the family data.

claim: There was no significant effect of gender on penetrance of SMAD6 mutations.
source: There was no significant effect of gender on penetrance.
evidence: This is a result from analysis of penetrance by gender.

claim: The rs1884302 risk allele frequency is 0.34 with an odds ratio of 4.6 for sagittal craniosynostosis.
source: A previous GWAS of non-syndromic sagittal craniosynostosis implicated common variants ~345 kb downstream of the closest gene, BMP2 (encoding bone morphogenetic protein 2), with unusually large effect size (e.g., rs1884302, with risk allele frequency of 0.34 and odds ratio of 4.6).
evidence: This is a statement about prior GWAS findings.

claim: BMP2 is a ligand for BMP receptors upstream of SMAD signaling.
source: BMP2 is a ligand for BMP receptors upstream of SMAD signaling (Salazar et al., 2016) and is an inducer of osteogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological function of BMP2 supported by a citation.

claim: BMP2 is an inducer of osteogenesis.
source: BMP2 is a ligand for BMP receptors upstream of SMAD signaling (Salazar et al., 2016) and is an inducer of osteogenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological function of BMP2.

claim: Fourteen individuals had both a SMAD6 mutation and the rs1884302 risk allele, and 100% of these had craniosynostosis.
source: Fourteen individuals had both a SMAD6 mutation and the rs1884302 risk allele; 100% of these had craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is a result from genotype-phenotype analysis in families.

claim: Sixteen subjects had a SMAD6 mutation but no rs1884302 risk allele, and only 3 of these individuals (19%) had craniosynostosis.
source: In contrast, 16 subjects had a SMAD6 mutation but no rs1884302 risk allele; only 3 of these individuals (19%) had craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is a result from genotype-phenotype analysis in families.

claim: Zero of 18 members of these kindreds who had only the rs1884302 risk allele had craniosynostosis.
source: Lastly, 0 of 18 members of these kindreds who had only the rs1884302 risk allele had craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is a result from genotype-phenotype analysis in families.

claim: The relationship of SMAD6 and BMP2 genotypes to craniosynostosis in these kindreds was highly significant (p=1.4 × 10^-10 by the Freeman-Halton extension of Fisher's exact test).
source: The relationship of these two genotypes to craniosynostosis in these kindreds was highly significant (p=1.4 × 10–10 by the Freeman-Halton extension of Fisher's exact test; Table 5).
evidence: This is a statistical result from association analysis.

claim: Among SMAD6 mutation carriers, the presence of the rs1884302 risk allele dramatically increased the occurrence of craniosynostosis (p=4.8 × 10^-6 by Fisher's exact test).
source: Confining analysis just to subjects with SMAD6 mutation, there was dramatically increased occurrence of craniosynostosis among those with the rs1884302 risk allele compared to those without (p=4.8 × 10–6 by Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from association analysis restricted to SMAD6 mutation carriers.

claim: The presence of the rs1884302 risk allele increased the risk of craniosynostosis more than 5-fold in SMAD6 mutation carriers.
source: The presence of the rs1884302 risk allele increased the risk of craniosynostosis >5-fold with a very high odds ratio that includes infinity owing to 100% penetrance among those with risk genotypes at both loci.
evidence: This is a result from calculating the effect of the BMP2 risk allele in SMAD6 mutation carriers.

claim: There was significant transmission disequilibrium, with rs1884302 risk alleles transmitted from heterozygous parents to affected offspring in 11 of 13 transmissions (p=0.013 by Chi-square).
source: This two locus contribution is further supported by significant transmission disequilibrium, with rs1884302 risk alleles transmitted from heterozygous parents to affected offspring in 11 of 13 transmissions (p=0.013 by Chi-square, Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This is a result from transmission disequilibrium test.

claim: Common variants at the BBS9 locus showed no significant interaction with SMAD6 (TDT p=0.89).
source: In contrast, common variants at the BBS9 locus that also showed strong association with midline craniosynostosis in case-control analysis (OR > 4) (Justice et al., 2012) showed no significant interaction with SMAD6 (TDT p=0.89; Supplementary file 1B), demonstrating specificity of the observed interaction of rare variants in SMAD6 and a common variant near BMP2.
evidence: This is a result from transmission disequilibrium test showing no interaction.

claim: The two locus linkage model provided extremely strong evidence supporting linkage with a maximum lod score of 7.37.
source: The results provided extremely strong evidence supporting linkage under a two locus model, with a maximum lod score of 7.37 (odds ratio 2.3 × 107:1 in favor of linkage compared to the null hypothesis; family-specific lod scores are shown in Supplementary file 1D).
evidence: This is a result from parametric linkage analysis.

claim: The maximum likelihood model specified 100% penetrance of craniosynostosis when risk alleles at both SMAD6 and BMP2 loci are present.
source: The maximum likelihood model specified 100% penetrance of craniosynostosis when risk alleles at both loci are present, 9% penetrance when only a damaging SMAD6 allele is present, 0.08% or 0.32% penetrance when only one or two BMP2 risk alleles are present, and a 0.02% phenocopy rate, with zero recombination between trait and both marker loci.
evidence: This describes the parameters of the maximum likelihood linkage model.

claim: The two locus model was 1410-fold more likely than the best single locus model.
source: This two locus model was 1410 – fold more likely than than the best single locus model, in which damaging SMAD6 variants had penetrance of 20%.
evidence: This is a result from comparing linkage models.

claim: SMAD6 mutations were significantly more frequent in kindreds with any metopic craniosynostosis (10 of 78, 12.8%) compared to those with isolated sagittal craniosynostosis (3 of 113, 2.7%; p=8.1 × 10^-3 by Fisher's exact test, odds ratio 5.3).
source: SMAD6 mutations were significantly more frequent in kindreds with any metopic craniosynostosis (10 of 78, 12.8%) compared to those with isolated sagittal craniosynostosis (3 of 113, 2.7%; p=8.1 × 10–3 by Fisher's exact test, odds ratio 5.3).
evidence: This is a result from comparing mutation frequencies across phenotypic subgroups.

claim: SMAD6 mutations confer greater risk for metopic suture closure.
source: These results suggest that mutations in SMAD6 confer greater risk for metopic suture closure.
evidence: This is an inference from the differential frequency of SMAD6 mutations in metopic vs. sagittal cases.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the type of mutation (LOF vs. D-mis) or location within SMAD6 and phenotypic class.
source: We found no significant correlation between the type of mutation (LOF vs. D-mis) or location within the gene of SMAD6 mutation and phenotypic class (Table 4).
evidence: This is a result from genotype-phenotype correlation analysis.

claim: Transmitted SMAD6 mutations were significantly enriched in kindreds with familial craniosynostosis, accounting for 4 of 17 kindreds with more than one affected subject (p=0.02, Fisher's exact test; odds ratio 5.6).
source: Interestingly, transmitted SMAD6 mutations were significantly enriched in kindreds with familial craniosynostosis, accounting for 4 of 17 kindreds with more than one affected subject (p=0.02, Fisher's exact test; odds ratio 5.6).
evidence: This is a result from comparing mutation frequencies in familial vs. sporadic cases.

claim: In kindreds with transmitted SMAD6 mutations, all four additional affected subjects carried the SMAD6 mutation found in the proband.
source: In these kindreds, all four additional affected subjects carried the SMAD6 mutation found in the proband (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a result from segregation analysis in familial cases.

claim: SMAD6 is a member of the inhibitory-SMAD family.
source: SMAD6 is a member of the inhibitory-SMAD family.
evidence: This is a statement about the classification of SMAD6.

claim: Activation of BMP receptors leads to phosphorylation of receptor SMADs, which can complex with SMAD4, translocate to the nucleus and partner with RUNX2 to induce transcription of genes that promote osteoblast differentiation.
source: Activation of BMP receptors leads to phosphorylation of receptor SMADs, which can complex with SMAD4, translocate to the nucleus and partner with RUNX2 to induce transcription of genes that promote osteoblast differentiation (Javed et al., 2008; Hata et al., 1998) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a description of the BMP signaling pathway supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 4a.

claim: SMAD6 inhibits BMP signaling by binding to phosphorylated receptor SMADs, forming an inactive complex.
source: This process is inhibited by SMAD6 binding to phosphorylated receptor SMADs, forming an inactive complex.
evidence: This is a description of SMAD6's inhibitory mechanism.

claim: SMAD6 also inhibits BMP signaling by complexing with the ubiquitin ligase SMURF1, which ubiquitylates BMP receptors, receptor SMADs and RUNX2, leading to their proteasomal degradation.
source: SMAD6 also inhibits BMP signaling by complexing with the ubiquitin ligase SMURF1, which ubiquitylates BMP receptors, receptor SMADs and RUNX2, leading to their proteasomal degradation (Figure 4b) (Murakami et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a description of another SMAD6 inhibitory mechanism supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 4b.

claim: In mice, constitutive activity of BMPR1A in cranial neural crest results in SMAD-dependent development of metopic craniosynostosis.
source: In mice, constitutive activity of BMPR1A in cranial neural crest results in SMAD-dependent development of metopic craniosynostosis (Komatsu et al., 2013), and genetic deficiency for the SMAD inhibitor SMURF1 causes midline craniosynostosis (Shimazu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about mouse model findings supported by a citation.

claim: Genetic deficiency for the SMAD inhibitor SMURF1 causes midline craniosynostosis in mice.
source: In mice, constitutive activity of BMPR1A in cranial neural crest results in SMAD-dependent development of metopic craniosynostosis (Komatsu et al., 2013), and genetic deficiency for the SMAD inhibitor SMURF1 causes midline craniosynostosis (Shimazu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a statement about mouse model findings supported by a citation.

claim: Duplication of RUNX2 causes syndromic metopic craniosynostosis in humans.
source: Similarly, duplication of RUNX2 causes syndromic metopic craniosynostosis in humans (Mefford et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a statement about human genetic findings supported by a citation.

claim: SMAD6 knockout mice are born with domed skulls and show anomalous bone deposition in the metopic suture.
source: Lastly, SMAD6 knockout mice are born with domed skulls and show anomalous bone deposition in the metopic suture; they also show an augmented and prolonged response to BMP2 stimulation (Estrada et al., 2011; Retting, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about mouse model findings supported by citations.

claim: SMAD6 knockout mice show an augmented and prolonged response to BMP2 stimulation.
source: Lastly, SMAD6 knockout mice are born with domed skulls and show anomalous bone deposition in the metopic suture; they also show an augmented and prolonged response to BMP2 stimulation (Estrada et al., 2011; Retting, 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about mouse model findings supported by citations.

claim: One de novo damaging missense mutation in SMURF1 was identified in a proband with sporadic metopic craniosynostosis.
source: Interestingly, we identified one de novo D-mis mutation in SMURF1 in a proband with sporadic metopic craniosynostosis (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a result from the exome sequencing analysis.

claim: One de novo LOF mutation was identified in both SPRY1 and SPRY4.
source: We identified one de novo LOF in both SPRY1 and SPRY4, developmental regulators of the MAP kinase/ERK pathway; these variants comprised two of only 11 de novo LOFs other than those in SMAD6.
evidence: This is a result from the exome sequencing analysis.

claim: SPRY1 and SPRY4 are developmental regulators of the MAP kinase/ERK pathway.
source: We identified one de novo LOF in both SPRY1 and SPRY4, developmental regulators of the MAP kinase/ERK pathway; these variants comprised two of only 11 de novo LOFs other than those in SMAD6.
evidence: This is a statement about the biological function of these genes.

claim: The probability of observing two or more de novo LOF mutations in any of the 4 Sprouty genes by chance in this cohort surpassed genome-wide significance (p=7.1 × 10^-7).
source: The probability of observing two or more de novo LOF mutations in any of the 4 Sprouty genes by chance in this cohort surpassed genome-wide significance (p=7.1 × 10–7, Table 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from gene set analysis.

claim: A de novo microdeletion that included SPRY1 has previously been reported in a child with sagittal craniosynostosis.
source: Consistent with a role for SPRY1 haploinsufficiency, a de novo microdeletion that included SPRY1 has previously been reported in a child with sagittal craniosynostosis (Fernández-Jaén et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about prior case report findings supported by a citation.

claim: In mice with TWIST1 haploinsufficiency, overexpression of SPRY1 prevents suture fusion.
source: Moreover, in mice with TWIST1 haploinsufficiency, a model of syndromic craniosynostosis, overexpression of SPRY1 prevents suture fusion (Connerney et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a statement about mouse model findings supported by a citation.

claim: Protein altering de novo mutations were identified in other regulators and mediators of MAP kinase signaling, including RASAL2, DUSP5, MAP3K8, KSR2, RPS6KA4, and RGS3.
source: Lastly, protein altering de novo mutations were also identified in other regulators and mediators of MAP kinase signaling, including RASAL2, DUSP5, MAP3K8, KSR2, RPS6KA4, and RGS3.
evidence: This is a result from the exome sequencing analysis.

claim: Five of 6 de novo mutations in MAP kinase pathway genes occurred in probands with sagittal craniosynostosis.
source: 5 of 6 occurred in probands with sagittal craniosynostosis (Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a result from analyzing the phenotypes associated with these mutations.

claim: SMAD6/BMP2 genotypes account for approximately 7% of probands in this cohort of non-syndromic midline craniosynostosis.
source: SMAD6 mutations with and without BMP2 risk alleles account for ~7% of probands in this cohort of non-syndromic midline craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is a calculation from the frequency of these genotypes in the cohort.

claim: SMAD6/BMP2 genotypes are inferred to account for approximately 3.5% of all craniosynostosis.
source: Moreover, because non-syndromic sagittal and metopic craniosynostosis comprise half of all craniosynostoses (Slater et al., 2008; Greenwood et al., 2014), SMAD6/BMP2 genotypes are inferred to account for ~3.5% of all craniosynostosis, and are likely rivaled in frequency only by mutations in FGFR2 as the most frequent cause of all craniosynostoses (Twigg and Wilkie, 2015).
evidence: This is an inference from the frequency in midline cases and the proportion of midline cases among all craniosynostosis.

claim: The combination of a rare damaging SMAD6 mutation plus a common BMP2 risk allele conferred 100% risk of craniosynostosis in the cohort.
source: The combination of a rare damaging SMAD6 mutation plus a common BMP2 risk allele conferred 100% risk of craniosynostosis in our cohort, while those with a SMAD6 mutation but no BMP2 risk allele were at markedly lower risk.
evidence: This is a result from the genotype-phenotype analysis in families.

claim: Subjects with a SMAD6 mutation but no BMP2 risk allele were at markedly lower risk of craniosynostosis.
source: The combination of a rare damaging SMAD6 mutation plus a common BMP2 risk allele conferred 100% risk of craniosynostosis in our cohort, while those with a SMAD6 mutation but no BMP2 risk allele were at markedly lower risk.
evidence: This is a result from the genotype-phenotype analysis in families.

claim: SMAD6 mutation-only cases thus far have all had isolated metopic craniosynostosis.
source: Interestingly, these SMAD6 mutation-only cases thus far have all had isolated metopic craniosynostosis (Figure 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the phenotypic analysis of cases with SMAD6 mutations but no BMP2 risk allele.

claim: Rare damaging SMAD6 mutations were found in nearly 25% of kindreds with recurrent midline craniosynostosis.
source: Rare damaging SMAD6 mutations were found in nearly 25% of kindreds with recurrent midline craniosynostosis, and 37.5% of patients with combined sagittal and metopic craniosynostosis in our cohort.
evidence: This is a result from analyzing mutation frequencies in specific phenotypic subgroups.

claim: Rare damaging SMAD6 mutations were found in 37.5% of patients with combined sagittal and metopic craniosynostosis.
source: Rare damaging SMAD6 mutations were found in nearly 25% of kindreds with recurrent midline craniosynostosis, and 37.5% of patients with combined sagittal and metopic craniosynostosis in our cohort.
evidence: This is a result from analyzing mutation frequencies in specific phenotypic subgroups.

claim: Eleven of 15 subjects with rare damaging SMAD6 variants who are more than one year of age had some form of developmental delay.
source: Considering neurodevelopmental outcomes, 11 of 15 subjects with rare damaging SMAD6 variants who are more than one year of age (and hence can have neurodevelopmental evaluation) had some form of developmental delay (Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: This is a result from clinical evaluation of subjects with SMAD6 mutations.

claim: More than a third of patients with non-syndromic midline craniosynostosis have subtle learning disability.
source: While early surgical intervention provides the best neurological outcomes (Patel et al., 2014), more than a third of patients with non-syndromic midline craniosynostosis have subtle learning disability (Magge et al., 2002; Shipster et al., 2003; Sidoti et al., 1996).
evidence: This is a statement about neurodevelopmental outcomes supported by citations.

claim: BMP signaling plays an essential role in vertebrate brain development.
source: BMP signaling plays an essential role in vertebrate brain development (Bier and De Robertis, 2015), raising the possibility that aberrant BMP signaling could contribute to neurodevelopmental outcome independent of its effect on craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is a statement about BMP signaling in development supported by a citation.

claim: Aberrant BMP signaling could contribute to neurodevelopmental outcome independent of its effect on craniosynostosis.
source: BMP signaling plays an essential role in vertebrate brain development (Bier and De Robertis, 2015), raising the possibility that aberrant BMP signaling could contribute to neurodevelopmental outcome independent of its effect on craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the role of BMP signaling in brain development.

claim: Congenital inguinal hernia was observed in 3 patients (16.7%) with SMAD6 mutations.
source: The only other clinical finding observed in more than one subject with SMAD6 mutation was a congenital inguinal hernia in 3 patients (16.7%; Supplementary file 1E).
evidence: This is a result from clinical evaluation of subjects with SMAD6 mutations.

claim: De novo protein-altering mutations are estimated to contribute to approximately 15% of cases, similar to estimates for autism and congenital heart disease.
source: While SMAD6 was the only single gene showing genome-wide significant burden of de novo mutation, de novo protein-altering mutations are estimated to contribute to ~15% of cases. This estimated fraction is similar to estimates for autism and congenital heart disease, other diseases in which large-scale studies have shown a role for de novo mutations (Homsy et al., 2015; Iossifov et al., 2014; Sanders et al., 2012; Zaidi et al., 2013; De Rubeis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a comparison of the contribution of de novo mutations across different diseases supported by citations.

claim: De novo mutation in a large number of genes are likely to contribute to sagittal and metopic craniosynostosis.
source: Also like autism and congenital heart disease, few individual genes were implicated after sequencing modest numbers of trios, implying that de novo mutation in a large number of genes are likely to contribute to sagittal and metopic craniosynostosis.
evidence: This is an inference from the pattern of de novo mutations observed.

claim: Duplication of a limb-specific enhancer near BMP2 increased BMP2 expression, leading to a Mendelian limb defect.
source: Moreover, consistent with the common variant near BMP2 modifying BMP2 expression, duplication of a nearby limb-specific enhancer increased BMP2 expression, leading to a Mendelian limb defect (Dathe et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a statement about prior findings supported by a citation, used to support the proposed mechanism.
